definition: A clause requiring you to protect the landlord from financial loss caused by your actions. If a guest is injured in your unit and sues, you — not the landlord — cover the costs.
If your insurer pays out a claim, this clause lets them sue the responsible party on your behalf to recover that money, preventing you from double-collecting.
Excuses either party from obligations when an extraordinary event occurs — natural disaster, pandemic, or government shutdown — that makes performance impossible.
A legal hold on a property by a third party (bank, contractor) who is owed money. A lien on your building could affect your tenancy if the landlord defaults.
A hidden flaw not visible during inspection — mold behind walls, faulty wiring, structural damage. Undisclosed latent defects may give you legal grounds for compensation.
Your legal right to a safe, clean, livable home. Landlords must maintain plumbing, heating, and structural integrity. Failure may let you withhold rent depending on local law.
Renting your unit to another person while you remain the primary tenant. Most leases either forbid this or require written landlord approval.
Failure by either party to meet a contract obligation — usually the tenant not paying rent. Default can trigger late fees, penalties, or eviction proceedings.
A right allowing a third party to use part of the property for a specific purpose, such as a utility company accessing pipes through shared corridors.
Money held by a neutral third party until a condition is met. Security deposits are often held in escrow to protect both tenant and landlord from disputes.
The fixed duration of the rental agreement — typically 6 or 12 months. Breaking the lease early usually incurs penalties specified in the contract.
A tenant who remains in the property after the lease expires without signing a renewal. Landlords can either accept this (creating a month-to-month tenancy) or pursue eviction.
A formal written notice from the landlord demanding the tenant vacate. The required notice period varies by jurisdiction — typically 30 to 90 days.
Money paid upfront, held by the landlord to cover unpaid rent or damages beyond normal wear and tear. Most jurisdictions require return within 14–30 days of move-out.
Minor deterioration expected from ordinary use — small scuffs, faded paint, worn carpet. Landlords cannot deduct this from your security deposit; only damage beyond this qualifies.
A rental arrangement with no fixed end date, automatically renewing each month. Either party can typically terminate with 30 days written notice.
The tenant pays a single flat rent and the landlord covers all operating expenses — utilities, insurance, property tax, maintenance.
The tenant pays base rent plus some or all operating costs. A triple net (NNN) lease has the tenant paying rent, utilities, insurance, and property taxes.
The landlord's right to enter your unit. Most jurisdictions require 24–48 hours written notice except in genuine emergencies.
Your right to use the property peacefully without interference from the landlord or anyone claiming ownership. Violation of this right may void the lease.
A binding promise in the lease — either something a party will do (positive covenant) or will not do (restrictive covenant), such as not running a business from the unit.
If you break the lease, this clause makes all remaining rent immediately due rather than month by month. Not enforceable in all jurisdictions.
Requires disputes to be settled by a private arbitrator instead of a court. This waives your right to sue in court and outcomes are typically binding and harder to appeal.

A pre-agreed sum specified in the lease as compensation for a specific breach, such as early termination. Courts may void these if the amount is deemed punitive rather than a genuine estimate of loss.
A signed statement confirming the lease terms are as written and no disputes exist. Often requested by banks or buyers when the property is being sold or refinanced.
When multiple tenants sign a lease, each is individually responsible for the full rent. If one tenant stops paying, the landlord can pursue any or all of the others for the full amount.
A third party (often a parent or employer) who co-signs the lease and agrees to cover rent if the tenant defaults. The guarantor is legally liable as if they were the tenant.
A partial month's rent calculated proportionally when you move in or out mid-month. For example, moving in on the 15th of a 30-day month means paying half a month's rent.
Transferring your entire lease to a new tenant, who takes over all your rights and obligations. Unlike subletting, you are released from the lease once assigned (if the landlord agrees).
When a landlord's failure to maintain habitable conditions effectively forces a tenant to leave. Courts may treat this as an eviction, entitling you to break the lease without penalty.
A legal action filed by a landlord to remove a tenant who refuses to vacate after proper notice. It is the formal court process for eviction.
A legal remedy allowing landlords in some jurisdictions to seize a tenant's property to recover unpaid rent. Largely abolished in many US states but still exists in others.
Local laws that limit how much a landlord can increase rent each year. Whether your unit qualifies depends on the building's age, location, and local ordinances.
Similar to rent control but typically applies to a broader set of units and allows small regulated increases annually rather than freezing rent entirely.
A tenancy with no fixed term, terminable by either party at any time with proper notice. Often what a holdover tenancy becomes if the landlord continues accepting rent.
Prohibits tenants from causing disturbances that interfere with other tenants' quiet enjoyment — excessive noise, illegal activity, or property damage.
Voluntarily giving up a contractual right. If a landlord consistently accepts late rent without penalty, they may be found to have waived their right to enforce the late fee.
Replacing one party in a contract with a new party, with all original parties agreeing. Used in lease assignments when the landlord formally releases the original tenant.
Improvements made to the property by the tenant that change its character — such as remodeling — without the landlord's consent. Even beneficial changes can be grounds for a lease violation.
A reduction or temporary suspension of rent, usually granted when the landlord fails to make required repairs or the unit becomes partially uninhabitable.
